text:
The reader who attends to what is missing from this passage is the one best rewarded. Sarah has no place anywhere in the chapter, and her death is announced in the verse which immediately follows it; the scene implies, though it nowhere states, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, and of Isaac nothing is said. The narrator withdraws his eye at the very moment when a lesser storyteller would have lingered, and the silence he leaves is itself a form of testimony.

It may be objected that the chapter shows no more than the common economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports what its persons feel and never explains them; and this may, in some measure, be granted. Restraint in such a narrator is nevertheless a kind of accusation, and his reticence here is deliberate. He knows what he withholds, for elsewhere he tells us plainly what his characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.
